title: Overview and justification
body:
This short course is about using AI as a tool for learning, and using it with a critical eye. You already know what generative AI tools are, and you have probably used one to study. The sharper question now is this: when you lean on AI, who is doing the thinking, you or the tool?

By the end you will be able to judge when AI genuinely supports your learning and when it quietly replaces it, read its output critically, name the ways it fails, and decide when not to use it at all. These are habits of judgement, not tricks, and you can use them this week in any subject.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this course, you will be able to:

_items.text: judge when using AI supports your learning and when it does the thinking for you
read AI output critically for accuracy, bias and what it leaves out
name the ways AI fails, and decide when it is wiser not to use it.

title: In real academic practice
body: Using AI to learn is already part of study in every subject. Tutors increasingly expect you to tell when a tool is building your understanding and when it is standing in for it, to question what it tells you, and to use it honestly. Build these habits now and they carry into every module, and into work where AI is a daily tool.

title: Signpost
body: The course has four short lessons. First, partner not answer machine: keeping yourself as the thinker. Second, reading AI critically: the checks that catch its errors. Third, knowing the failure modes: the named ways AI output goes wrong. Fourth, your responsible-use judgement: using AI well, and knowing when not to. Work through them in order; each builds on the one before.

title: Course instructions
body:
Start and finish with a confidence check. Before the lessons, you'll rate how confident you feel about each part of this topic. You'll rate the same statements again at the end, so you can see what has changed. Your ratings are yours: they aren't marked and no one else sees them.

The activities in the lessons are for practice. Questions, examples and reflective prompts are there to help you think, and they don't count towards passing. Reflective prompts are private and optional.

The test at the end is the one that counts. To complete the course you need to take the final test and score at least 70%. You can retake it.

title: How this course works
body:
The examples and activities in this course use invented people, authors and sources to show how things work. Unless we say otherwise, any name, citation or reference you meet in an example is fictional.

Where a lesson draws on real work, you'll find it listed under Lesson Sources at the bottom of that page. Every real source used in the course is gathered under Course Sources at the end.

title: Orientation
body: You have probably used an AI chatbot to help with study already. The harder skill is holding on to your own thinking while you do it. Used well, AI is a partner that helps you understand more; used carelessly, it becomes an answer machine that thinks in your place. This lesson is about telling the two apart, so you stay the one doing the learning.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: At this level the aim is not to relearn what AI is, but to use it with judgement. The test to carry through the whole course is a simple question: who is doing the thinking here, you or the tool? Asking it honestly, task by task, is what keeps AI a support to your learning rather than a substitute for it.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: explain what over-reliance on AI costs your learning, and ask who is doing the thinking
place your own use of AI against the four levels of AI literacy
judge, for a task in {{context}}, what AI can and cannot do for you.

title: Concept: definition
body:
AI can genuinely help you learn. It can explain an idea several ways, break down a hard topic, give you practice questions, and present an unfamiliar subject in plain language. The risk is over-reliance: letting the tool do the thinking that the learning depends on. University is meant to build your critical thinking, your judgement and your ability to work a problem through. Lean on AI for those, and you hand away the very skills you are there to develop.

So the useful question is not whether AI is good or bad, but who is doing the thinking. A tool that helps you understand a concept supports your learning. A tool that hands you a finished answer you cannot explain has replaced it. The same chatbot can do either, depending on how you use it.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Think of a recent time you used AI to study. Looking back, who was doing the thinking - you or the tool? Would you use it the same way again?
instruction: Write a few sentences for yourself. This is not marked, and there are no right answers.

title: Summary
displayTitle: Summary
body: AI can help you learn, but only if you stay the one doing the thinking. Over-reliance hands away the critical thinking, judgement and problem-solving that university is meant to build. You can now explain what over-reliance costs, place your own use against the four levels of AI literacy, and judge what a tool can and cannot do for a given task. The next lesson turns to the single most important skill: reading AI output critically.

title: Orientation
body: Once you decide a tool can help, the next skill matters more than any other: reading what it gives you with a critical eye. AI tools do not flag their own mistakes. They write a wrong answer in the same confident voice as a right one, so the judgement about what to trust has to come from you.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: Critical evaluation is the single most important skill in using AI to learn. It is not about distrusting everything, but about testing claims before you rely on them. At this level you are expected to check AI output the way you would weigh any source: against the evidence, against your own reading, and against what it quietly leaves out.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: evaluate an AI answer for accuracy, sources, bias and what it leaves out
recognise the failure patterns that make confident output untrustworthy
apply good checking habits to AI output in {{context}}.

title: Concept: definition
body:
Reading AI critically means four moves. You fact-check the content against a source you trust. You verify every source the tool offers, because tools invent references that look real. You detect bias by asking whose view the answer reflects. And you spot omission: the caveat or counter-argument the tool quietly dropped.

Certain failure patterns make this easier. Be suspicious of exact statistics and percentages, which are often fabricated. Remember that a confident tone is not evidence of accuracy. Check how current the information is, since tools have a training cut-off. If an answer sounds too perfect, dig into it. And where a tool contradicts your academic sources, trust the sources.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Think of a time an AI answer sounded completely convincing. Looking back, what in it would you now want to check before trusting it?
instruction: Write a few sentences for yourself. This is not marked, and there are no right answers.

title: Summary
displayTitle: Summary
body: Critical evaluation is the single most important skill in using AI to learn. You fact-check the content, verify every source, detect bias, and spot what has been left out, treating a confident tone as no proof of accuracy. You can now evaluate an AI answer, recognise the failure patterns that should make you suspicious, and apply steady checking habits. The next lesson names the specific ways AI output goes wrong.

title: Orientation
body: Knowing that AI can be wrong is one thing; knowing how it goes wrong is sharper. Its mistakes fall into a handful of recognisable patterns. Once you can name them, you can spot them, and a vague unease about an answer turns into a specific thing to check.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: This lesson gives you a vocabulary for AI's failures. Each pattern has a name and a tell. At this level you are expected to look at a piece of AI output and say not just that something feels off, but which failure mode is at work and how you would check for it.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: name the main ways AI output fails, from hallucination to quiet omission
analyse a piece of AI output to identify which failure mode is at work
spot the failure modes most likely to catch you out in {{context}}.

title: Concept: definition
body:
AI output fails in patterns, not at random, and each pattern has a name. Hallucination is fabricated content: invented facts, authors or citations. Bias is the prejudice a tool absorbs from its training data. Plausible nonsense sounds authoritative but means nothing on a close read. False precision dresses a guess as an exact figure.

Four more complete the picture. Oversimplification flattens a complex idea into something neat but wrong. Outdated information reflects the tool's training cut-off. Context collapse is right information applied to the wrong situation. And omission is the quiet dropping of caveats and counter-arguments. Name the pattern, and you know what to check.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Look back at an AI answer you have used. Which of the eight failure modes could it have contained, and would you have noticed at the time?
instruction: Write a few sentences for yourself. This is not marked, and there are no right answers.

title: Summary
displayTitle: Summary
body: AI output fails in named patterns: hallucination, bias, plausible nonsense, false precision, oversimplification, outdated information, context collapse and omission. Once you can name them, a vague unease becomes a specific thing to check. You can now name the main failure modes, analyse an answer to see which is at work, and spot the ones most likely to catch you out. The last lesson draws this together into responsible judgement about when, and whether, to use AI at all.

title: Course summary
body: You have reached the end of the course. Using AI to learn is no longer a matter of habit: it is something you do with judgement. You can stay the one doing the thinking, read what a tool gives you critically, name the ways its output fails, and decide when to use AI and when to keep it out. Look back at the confidence check: comparing where you started with where you are now shows how far this has moved.

title: In real academic practice
body: From here, using AI critically is something you practise in every module. Each judgement about whether a tool fits, each answer you check before trusting it, each time you keep AI out of a task that needs your own thinking, is this skill at work. It is also what study and working life increasingly reward: people who use these tools with judgement, and know when not to.

title: Where this goes next
body: Two directions build on this. Going deeper: the advanced AI and technology course takes you into prompting skilfully to learn, creating substantial work with AI, and the wider ethics of its use. Going wider: these habits support every other pathway, from Academic Writing and Criticality to Researching, wherever you bring a tool into real academic work.

title: Explore AI literacy
displayTitle: The four levels of AI literacy
body: AI literacy means understanding what AI can do, where it falls short, and how to use it responsibly. It grows through four levels. Open each one to see what it involves, and notice where your own use sits.
instruction: Open any level to read it. You can keep more than one open at once.

_items.title: Basic: knowing what AI is
_items.body: You understand what generative AI is and roughly how it works: it predicts likely patterns in language rather than looking up facts.
_items.advice: In practice: you can tell a classmate, in plain terms, that a chatbot writes by predicting words, not by knowing things.

_items.title: Intermediate: using tools to learn
_items.body: You can use AI tools effectively to support your study, such as explaining a concept, summarising a text, or generating practice questions.
_items.advice: In practice: you bring a tool into a task on purpose, to help you understand something, and you still do the understanding yourself.

_items.title: Advanced: evaluating the output
_items.body: You critically evaluate what a tool gives you, checking it for accuracy and bias, and you understand the ethical questions around AI use.
_items.advice: In practice: you treat every answer as a draft to test, not a fact to trust, and you notice what it quietly leaves out.

_items.title: Professional: responsible integration
_items.body: You integrate AI responsibly into real work, judging when it fits, directing it well, and taking responsibility for what you produce with it.
_items.advice: In practice: you decide where a tool belongs in a piece of work, and you can explain and defend every choice you made with it.

title: Formative check: matching AI to the task
displayTitle: Who is doing the thinking?
body: Using AI for learning means using it to deepen your understanding, not to hand you an answer. Aim for understanding-seeking prompts, where you still do the thinking.
instruction: Select every prompt where you are doing the thinking. More than one applies.
ariaQuestion: Select every prompt where you, not the tool, are doing the thinking.

_items.text: Help me understand the main debates in this topic so I can write my own introduction.
_items.feedback: Yes. AI builds your understanding and you still do the writing.

_items.text: Write the introduction on this topic for me.
_items.feedback: No. The tool produces the work and you only receive a product.

_items.text: Quiz me on this week's reading and tell me what I got wrong.
_items.feedback: Yes. You attempt the answers, so the thinking stays with you.

_items.text: Give me three points I can paste straight into my essay.
_items.feedback: No. Pasting AI's points in means the tool did the thinking.

_items.text: Here is my explanation of the idea. What have I misunderstood?
_items.feedback: Yes. You explain first, then use AI to check you.

_items.text: Answer the assignment question for me.
_items.feedback: No. This hands the whole task to the tool.

_feedback.correct: Spot on. Each one you chose keeps the thinking with you. AI supports the process and you build the knowledge.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the prompts where you think first and AI only checks or supports you. Try again.
_incorrect.final: The understanding-seeking prompts are the ones where you do the work and AI helps. The others hand the task to the tool.

_partlyCorrect.notFinal: Close. You have some right. Look again for any prompt that hands the whole task to the tool. Try again.
_partlyCorrect.final: Close. The understanding-seeking prompts are the ones where you do the thinking and AI supports you.

title: Worked example
displayTitle: Worked example
body:
Two students are revising the same difficult theory for an exam.

{{learner-a}} asks a chatbot to explain the theory and summarise the key points, then rereads the summary until it feels familiar. It all makes sense on the screen. In the exam, asked to apply the theory to a new case, {{learner-a}} cannot do it: the tool had done the thinking, and the understanding was never built. The summary was the tool's, not {{learner-a}}'s.

{{learner-b}} uses the same chatbot to explain the theory, then closes it and writes the explanation out from memory in their own words. {{learner-b}} asks the tool what the explanation missed, fixes the gaps, and works through a practice case. The tool helped {{learner-b}} learn; it did not learn in {{learner-b}}'s place.

Both used AI to revise. Only {{learner-b}} stayed the one doing the thinking, and so could use the theory when it counted.

title: Before you let AI help
displayTitle: Checklist: Who is doing the thinking?
body: These questions keep you the one who learns. Run through them before and during any use of AI to study.
instruction: Tick each item once you have considered it.

_items.text: Have I asked who is doing the thinking on this task, me or the tool?
Am I using AI to understand something, or to avoid understanding it?
Could I explain this in my own words with the tool closed?
Is this a skill the task is meant to build in me?
Where does my use sit on the four levels of AI literacy?

title: Formative check: matching AI to the task
displayTitle: Which use of an AI tool most clearly means the tool, not you, is doing the thinking?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which use most clearly means the tool is doing the thinking?

_items.text: Asking it to write an answer you then submit without being able to explain it.
_items.feedback: Yes. If you cannot explain the answer, the tool did the thinking, not you.

_items.text: Asking it to explain a concept several ways so you can test your own understanding.
_items.feedback: This supports your learning; you still do the understanding.

_items.text: Asking it for practice questions that you attempt yourself.
_items.feedback: Attempting practice yourself keeps the thinking with you.

_items.text: Asking it to break a hard topic into smaller parts you then study.
_items.feedback: Breaking a topic down to study it yourself supports your learning.

_feedback.correct: That's right. An answer you cannot explain is one the tool thought through for you.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the use where the tool produces the thinking, not just support for it.
_incorrect.final: Submitting an answer you cannot explain means the tool did the thinking. Explaining, practising and breaking a topic down all keep the thinking with you.

title: Formative check: help versus short-circuit
displayTitle: In the worked example, why was the second student still able to use the theory in the exam?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Why could the second student use the theory in the exam?

_items.text: They used the tool to help them learn, then built the understanding themselves.
_items.feedback: Yes. The tool supported the learning; the understanding was theirs.

_items.text: They used a more advanced chatbot than the first student.
_items.feedback: The tool was not the difference; how it was used was.

_items.text: They asked the tool to summarise the theory more carefully.
_items.feedback: A better summary still leaves the thinking with the tool.

_items.text: They revised for longer using the tool.
_items.feedback: Time was not the point; who did the thinking was.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The second student let the tool support learning rather than do it.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about who built the understanding.
_incorrect.final: The second student used the tool to help them learn, then did the understanding themselves. A better tool, a better summary or more time are not the difference.

title: Formative check: deciding on a task
displayTitle: You are working on a task in {{context}}. Which response shows the Advanced level of AI literacy?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which response shows the Advanced level of AI literacy?

_items.text: You treat the tool's answer as a draft to test for accuracy and bias before using any of it.
_items.feedback: Yes. Critically evaluating the output is the Advanced level.

_items.text: You accept the answer because it is detailed and sounds confident.
_items.feedback: A confident tone is not evidence; this skips the evaluation.

_items.text: You avoid AI entirely because it cannot be trusted at all.
_items.feedback: A blanket ban is not evaluation; the Advanced level is about judging output.

_items.text: You use whatever the tool gives, since checking takes too long in {{context}}.
_items.feedback: Skipping the check is the opposite of the Advanced level.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Testing output for accuracy and bias is critical evaluation, the Advanced level of AI literacy.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. The Advanced level is about evaluating output, not trusting it or avoiding AI altogether.
_incorrect.final: Treating the answer as a draft to test for accuracy and bias is the Advanced level. Trusting a confident tone, avoiding AI, or skipping the check are not.

title: Rely on it, or check it?
displayTitle: Rely on it, or check it?
body: For each thing you might get from an AI tool, predict whether you can rely on it or must always verify it. Turn the card to check.
instruction: Select each card to turn it over.

front.title: Rephrasing a passage you already have in plainer words

back.title: Fairly safe to rely on
back.body: Rewording text you can see is low-risk. Still read the result against the original to be sure the meaning held.

front.title: Generating practice questions on a topic

back.title: Fairly safe to rely on
back.body: Making practice questions is a good fit. Attempt them yourself, then check the answers against your materials.

front.title: Explaining a concept in several different ways

back.title: Fairly safe to rely on
back.body: Different explanations suit a tool well. Afterwards, test your understanding with the tool closed.

front.title: An exact statistic or percentage it states

back.title: Always verify
back.body: Tools fabricate precise figures with full confidence. Never quote a number you have not checked against a real source.

front.title: A reference or citation it gives you

back.title: Always verify
back.body: Tools invent real-looking authors, titles and years. Look up every reference before you cite it.

front.title: A one-paragraph summary of a debated topic

back.title: Always verify
back.body: Tools drop caveats and minority views. Ask what the summary leaves out before you rely on it.

title: Worked example
displayTitle: Worked example
body:
Two students ask a chatbot to summarise the evidence on a contested question for an essay.

{{learner-a}} gets a fluent summary with a striking statistic and three named studies. It reads as though an expert wrote it, so {{learner-a}} builds the essay around the figure and cites the studies. The statistic was invented, one study does not exist, and only one side of the debate appears. None of it was checked, and the essay rests on things that were never true.

{{learner-b}} gets a similar summary and treats it as a set of leads, not facts. {{learner-b}} tries to verify the statistic and cannot find it, checks each study in the library, and notices the summary ignores a major counter-argument. {{learner-b}} keeps what holds up, drops the rest, and reads more widely to fill the gap.

Both got the same confident answer. Only {{learner-b}} read it critically, and so caught the invented figure, the false source and the missing side.

title: Before you trust an answer
displayTitle: Checklist: Four checks to run
body: Run these on anything a tool gives you before it goes near your work.
instruction: Tick each item once you have tried it.

_items.text: Have I fact-checked each claim against a source I trust?
Have I looked up every reference to confirm it exists and says what the tool claimed?
Have I asked whose view this reflects, and what it leaves out?
Am I treating confident wording as proof of accuracy?
If this contradicts my academic sources, am I trusting the sources?

title: Formative check: a clear prompt
displayTitle: An AI answer includes a precise statistic that would strengthen your argument. What should you do?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What should you do with a precise statistic from an AI answer?

_items.text: Treat it as unverified and check it against a real source before using it.
_items.feedback: Yes. Exact figures are often fabricated, so verify before using.

_items.text: Use it, because an exact figure shows the tool has specific data.
_items.feedback: An exact figure is often false precision, not real data.

_items.text: Use it, because the answer is detailed and confidently written.
_items.feedback: Confident wording is not evidence of accuracy.

_items.text: Use it, as long as you reword the sentence around it.
_items.feedback: Rewording an unchecked figure does not make it true.

_feedback.correct: That's right. A precise statistic must be verified against a real source before you rely on it.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Precision and confidence are not proof; the figure needs checking.
_incorrect.final: You treat the statistic as unverified and check it against a real source. Exactness, confidence and rewording do not make a figure true.

title: Formative check: refining a prompt
displayTitle: In the worked example, what made the second student's reading of the summary critical?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What made the second student's reading critical?

_items.text: They verified the statistic and sources and noticed a missing side, instead of trusting the fluent answer.
_items.feedback: Yes. Checking claims and spotting omission is critical reading.

_items.text: They used a different tool to write the summary.
_items.feedback: The tool was not the point; the checking was.

_items.text: They trusted the summary because it was detailed.
_items.feedback: Trusting detail is the opposite of reading critically.

_items.text: They read the summary more quickly.
_items.feedback: Speed is not the point; testing the content is.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Verifying the claims and noticing what was missing is critical reading.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look at what the second student tested and what they noticed.
_incorrect.final: The second student verified the figure and sources and spotted a missing side. The tool, blind trust or reading speed are not the difference.

title: Formative check: building a prompt
displayTitle: You ask a tool to summarise a debate in {{context}}. What is the best way to read the summary critically?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What is the best way to read a summary critically?

_items.text: Ask whose perspective it reflects and what views or evidence it leaves out.
_items.feedback: Yes. Checking perspective and omission is how you read for bias.

_items.text: Accept it if it is long, detailed and neutral in tone.
_items.feedback: Length and a neutral tone are not the same as balance.

_items.text: Trust it because a tool has read more on {{context}} than any person could.
_items.feedback: Wide reading does not make a summary balanced.

_items.text: Assume it is balanced because it does not take an obvious side.
_items.feedback: No obvious side can still hide a one-sided picture.

_feedback.correct: That's right. You read for bias by asking whose view the summary reflects and what it leaves out.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Length, tone and breadth are not balance.
_incorrect.final: You ask whose perspective the summary reflects and what it leaves out. Length, a neutral tone and wide reading do not make it balanced.

title: Explore the failure modes
displayTitle: The eight ways AI output goes wrong
body: Each of these is a named way AI output fails. Open each one to see what it means and what it looks like.
instruction: Select each heading to reveal it. Work through all eight.

_items.title: Hallucination
_items.body: The tool states things that are simply made up: invented facts, events, authors or citations, presented as real. It is the most common and most damaging failure, because the fabrication looks exactly like genuine content.

_items.title: Bias and discrimination
_items.body: The tool reproduces prejudice from its training data, favouring some groups, views or regions over others. The result can look neutral while quietly skewing whose perspective counts.

_items.title: Plausible nonsense
_items.body: The answer sounds authoritative and well formed, but on a close read it means little or nothing. Fluent wording hides the fact that no real substance sits underneath.

_items.title: False precision
_items.body: A rough guess is dressed up as an exact figure: a specific percentage, a precise date, a neat statistic. The precision feels convincing, but the number was never real.

_items.title: Oversimplification
_items.body: A complex idea is flattened into something neat and tidy that loses what mattered. The answer is easy to read and quietly wrong, because the nuance has been stripped out.

_items.title: Outdated information
_items.body: The tool answers from a training cut-off in the past, so recent developments are missing or wrong. It rarely tells you how current it is, so it can state old information as if it were today's.

_items.title: Context collapse
_items.body: The information is right in general but wrong for your situation: the correct answer to a slightly different question. It fits a textbook case, not the specific one in front of you.

_items.title: Omission
_items.body: The caveats, exceptions and counter-arguments are quietly dropped, leaving a one-sided picture. What is missing can mislead you as much as anything the tool actually got wrong.

title: Worked example
displayTitle: Worked example
body:
Two students get the same AI-written answer for an assignment: a confident paragraph with a precise statistic, a named source, and a tidy conclusion.

{{learner-a}} reads it, finds nothing obviously wrong, and uses it whole. The exact figure was false precision, the source was a hallucination, and the tidy conclusion was an oversimplification that dropped every exception. Because {{learner-a}} could not name these failures, none of them were spotted, and all three went into the work.

{{learner-b}} reads the same paragraph against the failure modes. The oddly exact figure looks like false precision and fails a check; the source cannot be found, which points to hallucination; the conclusion feels too neat, a sign of oversimplification. Little of the paragraph survives, and the work is stronger for it.

Both saw the same answer. Only {{learner-b}} had the names for what was wrong, and so knew exactly what to check.

title: When an answer looks off
displayTitle: Checklist: How to pin down the failure
body: When something about an AI answer feels wrong, use these to name it and check it.
instruction: Tick each item once you have tried it.

_items.text: Could any fact, author or citation here be hallucinated?
Is an exact figure really false precision dressed as data?
Does a neat, confident answer actually make sense on a close read?
Has a complex point been oversimplified, or a caveat omitted?
Could this be right in general but wrong for my situation?
Might the information be out of date?

title: Formative check: checking accuracy
displayTitle: An AI answer gives '73.4% of students' with no source you can find. Which failure mode is this most likely to be?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which failure mode does an unsourced exact statistic suggest?

_items.text: False precision, and very possibly a hallucinated figure.
_items.feedback: Yes. An oddly exact, unsourced number is classic false precision.

_items.text: Context collapse, because the figure is from another subject.
_items.feedback: Context collapse is right information in the wrong situation, not an invented number.

_items.text: Outdated information, because the figure predates the cut-off.
_items.feedback: An old figure would still be real; this one has no source at all.

_items.text: Bias, because the figure favours one group.
_items.feedback: Bias is skewed perspective, not a fabricated statistic.

_feedback.correct: That's right. A suspiciously exact, unsourced figure is false precision, often hiding a hallucination.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what an oddly exact, unverifiable number signals.
_incorrect.final: An exact, unsourced figure is false precision, very possibly hallucinated. Context collapse, outdated information and bias are different failures.

title: Formative check: spotting bias
displayTitle: In the worked example, why did the second student catch failures the first student missed?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Why did the second student catch the failures?

_items.text: They read the answer against the named failure modes, so they knew what to check.
_items.feedback: Yes. Names for the failures turned unease into specific checks.

_items.text: They were given a different, more accurate answer.
_items.feedback: The answer was the same; the reading was different.

_items.text: They trusted the paragraph because it looked tidy.
_items.feedback: Trusting a tidy answer is how the failures slip through.

_items.text: They avoided using AI at all.
_items.feedback: They did use AI; they just read its output critically.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Naming the failure modes let the second student check for each one.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what let the second student know where to look.
_incorrect.final: The second student read the answer against the named failure modes and so knew what to check. The answer, blind trust or avoiding AI are not the reason.

title: Formative check: using AI with integrity
displayTitle: Which failure mode is most likely to catch you out when using AI for a topic in {{context}}?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which failure mode is most likely to catch you out?

_items.text: Omission: the tool gives a confident answer but quietly drops the exceptions and counter-arguments that matter in {{context}}.
_items.feedback: Yes. What is left out can mislead as much as an outright error.

_items.text: The tool refusing to answer questions about {{context}} at all.
_items.feedback: A refusal is obvious; it does not quietly damage your work.

_items.text: The tool writing in a style too formal for {{context}}.
_items.feedback: Style is easy to fix and is not a failure of accuracy.

_items.text: The tool producing answers too quickly to read in {{context}}.
_items.feedback: Speed is not a failure mode.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Omission is easy to miss, because what is dropped is invisible unless you look for it.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. A refusal, an over-formal style or speed are not the failures that quietly damage your work.
_incorrect.final: Omission is the real risk: a confident answer that drops the caveats and counter-arguments that matter. What is missing can mislead as much as an error.

displayTitle: Which use of an AI tool most clearly means the tool, not the student, is doing the thinking?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which use most clearly means the tool is doing the thinking?

_items.text: Submitting an AI-written answer the student cannot explain in their own words.
_items.feedback: Yes. An answer you cannot explain is one the tool thought through.

_items.text: Asking it to explain a concept so the student can then test their own understanding.
_items.feedback: This supports learning; the student still does the understanding.

_items.text: Asking it for practice questions the student attempts alone.
_items.feedback: Attempting practice keeps the thinking with the student.

_items.text: Asking it to reword a paragraph the student has already written.
_items.feedback: Rewording the student's own text does not replace the thinking.

_feedback.correct: That's right. An answer the student cannot explain is one the tool did the thinking for.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the use where the tool produces the thinking, not just support for it.

displayTitle: A student critically evaluates AI output and understands the ethics of using it. Which level of AI literacy does this describe?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which level of AI literacy is critical evaluation of output?

_items.text: Advanced.
_items.feedback: Yes. Critical evaluation of output is the Advanced level.

_items.text: Basic, because they know what AI is.
_items.feedback: Basic is only knowing what AI is and how it works.

_items.text: Intermediate, because they can use the tools.
_items.feedback: Intermediate is using tools effectively, not yet evaluating them.

_items.text: No level, because literacy is only about using the tools.
_items.feedback: Evaluating and using responsibly are higher levels of literacy.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Critically evaluating output and understanding its ethics is the Advanced level.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about which level is about judging output rather than just using tools.

displayTitle: An AI answer includes a precise statistic that would help your argument. What should you do before using it?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What should you do before using a precise statistic from AI?

_items.text: Treat it as unverified and check it against a real source.
_items.feedback: Yes. Exact figures are often fabricated, so verify first.

_items.text: Use it, because an exact figure shows the tool has real data.
_items.feedback: An exact figure is often false precision, not real data.

_items.text: Use it, because the answer is confidently written.
_items.feedback: Confident wording is not evidence of accuracy.

_items.text: Use it, as long as you reword the sentence around it.
_items.feedback: Rewording an unchecked figure does not make it true.

_feedback.correct: That's right. A precise statistic must be verified against a real source first.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Precision and confidence are not proof; the figure needs checking.

displayTitle: A tool gives you three references in perfect format. Before citing them you should...
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What should you do before citing a tool's references?

_items.text: look each one up to confirm it exists and says what the tool claimed.
_items.feedback: Yes. Tools invent citations, so each must be verified.

_items.text: cite them all, since the format is correct.
_items.feedback: Correct format does not make a reference real.

_items.text: cite only the most recent ones.
_items.feedback: A recent year does not confirm a source exists.

_items.text: trust them because the names look plausible.
_items.feedback: Plausible names are what invented references have.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Every reference must be looked up and confirmed before you cite it.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what proves a reference is real.

displayTitle: An AI answer gives '73.4% of cases' with no source you can find. Which failure mode is this most likely to be?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which failure mode is an unsourced exact statistic?

_items.text: False precision, very possibly with a hallucinated figure.
_items.feedback: Yes. An oddly exact, unsourced number is false precision.

_items.text: Context collapse.
_items.feedback: Context collapse is right information in the wrong situation.

_items.text: Outdated information.
_items.feedback: An old figure would still be real; this one has no source.

_items.text: Oversimplification.
_items.feedback: Oversimplification flattens an idea; it does not invent a number.

_feedback.correct: That's right. A suspiciously exact, unsourced figure is false precision, often hiding a hallucination.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what an oddly exact, unverifiable number signals.

displayTitle: A tool summarises a debated topic but drops every caveat and counter-argument. Which failure mode is this?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which failure mode is dropping caveats and counter-arguments?

_items.text: Omission.
_items.feedback: Yes. Quietly dropping caveats and counter-arguments is omission.

_items.text: False precision.
_items.feedback: False precision is a fabricated exact figure, not a missing side.

_items.text: Hallucination.
_items.feedback: Hallucination is invented content, not a dropped caveat.

_items.text: Plausible nonsense.
_items.feedback: Plausible nonsense is fluent but empty, not one-sided.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Dropping the caveats and counter-arguments is omission.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about the failure where what is left out is the problem.

title: Orientation
body: You have looked at staying the thinker, reading AI critically, and naming its failure modes. This final lesson brings them together into a single question of judgement: how do you use AI responsibly, and how do you know when not to use it at all? Responsible use protects four things at once - your learning, your integrity, your privacy, and the wider world.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: At this stage you are not expected to get every call right. The aim is to see responsible use as one judgement that weighs several things together, and to carry it into the rest of your studies. Knowing when to keep AI out of a task is as much a skill as knowing how to use it.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: weigh how a use of AI affects your learning, integrity, privacy and the environment
judge when AI is the wrong tool, and when not to use it at all
decide, for a task in {{context}}, how to use AI responsibly or whether to use it.

title: Concept: definition
body:
Responsible use means protecting four things at once. Protect your learning: ask whether a tool adds value, use it to spark ideas rather than replace thinking, and always do the substantive reading yourself. Protect your integrity: never pass off AI text as your own, let your thinking lead, and own any error or bias you include. Protect your privacy: assume anything you enter may be stored, so never paste personal, sensitive or copyrighted material. And protect the wider world: AI uses real energy and water, so ask whether it is the right tool for the job.

Part of responsible use is knowing when not to use AI at all. Keep it out when you need deep, uninterrupted thinking, when the struggle itself is where the learning happens, when you do not understand its output, or when you are simply putting off the real work. Not understanding an answer is a reason to stop, not a reason to carry on.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Think of a task coming up where you could use AI. Weigh it up: would using AI protect or harm your learning, and is this a time to use it or to keep it out?
instruction: Write a few sentences for yourself. This is not marked, and the questions have no right answers.

title: Summary
displayTitle: Summary
body: Responsible use is one judgement that protects four things at once: your learning, your integrity, your privacy, and the wider world. Part of that judgement is knowing when not to use AI at all - when the struggle is the learning, or when you do not understand what it gives you. Across the course you have learned to stay the thinker, read AI critically, name its failure modes, and now to weigh all of this into a single decision you can defend. That judgement is what carries into the rest of your studies.

title: Four things to protect
displayTitle: Four things to protect
body: Responsible use means protecting four things at once. Select each part to see what it asks of you.
instruction: Select each part of the cycle.

_items.title: Your learning
_items.body: Ask whether the tool adds real value, use it to spark ideas rather than replace thinking, and always do the substantive reading yourself.

_items.title: Your integrity
_items.body: Never pass off AI text as your own. Let your thinking lead, reference and declare any AI use, and own any error or bias you include.

_items.title: Privacy and IP
_items.body: Assume anything you enter may be stored or reused, so never paste personal, sensitive or copyrighted material into a tool.

_items.title: The environment
_items.body: AI uses real energy and water. Ask whether it is the best tool for the job, and reach for a simpler one when that would do.

title: Worked example
displayTitle: Worked example
body:
Two students face the same week: a reflective essay on their own learning, and a dense set of readings to get through.

{{learner-a}} puts both into a chatbot. The reflective essay comes back fluent but generic, with none of {{learner-a}}'s own experience in it, and the readings become a summary {{learner-a}} never actually reads. A sensitive placement detail goes into the tool along the way. The work is finished, but little was learned and something private was shared.

{{learner-b}} judges each task on its own. The reflection is personal and is the point of the exercise, so {{learner-b}} writes it alone. For the readings, {{learner-b}} uses the tool to clarify two hard passages, does the reading itself, and keeps every personal detail out of the tool.

Both had the same tools and the same deadline. Only {{learner-b}} used AI where it helped, kept it out where it did not, and protected both the learning and their privacy.

title: A responsible-use check
displayTitle: Checklist: Before, and instead of, using AI
body: Run through these whenever you are about to bring AI into a piece of work.
instruction: Tick each item when you have considered it.

_items.text: Does using AI here add real value, or would it just replace my thinking?
Can I keep my integrity: own the work, reference and declare any use?
Am I about to enter anything personal, sensitive or copyrighted?
Is a simpler, lower-impact tool good enough for this?
Is this a task I should do without AI, because the struggle is the learning?
Do I actually understand the output, or is that a sign to stop?

displayTitle: Why is it better to treat responsible AI use as one judgement rather than a single rule like 'always declare it'?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Why treat responsible use as one judgement rather than a single rule?

_items.text: Because a use can be declared yet still harm your learning, privacy or the environment, so several things must be weighed at once.
_items.feedback: Yes. One rule cannot protect everything responsible use has to protect.

_items.text: Because declaring AI use is never necessary once you use it responsibly.
_items.feedback: Declaring use is often part of responsible use, not something it removes.

_items.text: Because one judgement means you no longer need to check the output.
_items.feedback: Checking the output stays part of the judgement.

_items.text: Because weighing things up takes less care than following a rule.
_items.feedback: It takes more care, not less; that is the point.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Responsible use weighs learning, integrity, privacy and impact together, which a single rule cannot.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about everything responsible use has to protect at once.
_incorrect.final: A declared use can still harm your learning or privacy, so responsible use weighs several things together. It does not remove declaring or checking, and it takes more care, not less.

displayTitle: In the worked example, what made the second student's use of AI responsible?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What made the second student's use responsible?

_items.text: They judged each task on its own, used AI where it helped, kept it out of the personal task, and protected their privacy.
_items.feedback: Yes. That is responsible use as one judgement, task by task.

_items.text: They used the tool for everything to save time.
_items.feedback: Using it for everything is the opposite of judging each task.

_items.text: They refused to use AI for any part of the work.
_items.feedback: They did use AI, where it genuinely helped.

_items.text: They put their private details into the tool to get a better answer.
_items.feedback: Sharing private details is exactly what responsible use avoids.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Judging each task and protecting both learning and privacy is responsible use.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look at how the second student decided task by task.
_incorrect.final: The second student judged each task on its own, used AI where it helped, kept it out of the personal task, and protected their privacy. Blanket use, a blanket ban or sharing private details are not responsible use.

displayTitle: You are planning your AI use for a term of study in {{context}}. Which plan best shows responsible judgement?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which plan best shows responsible judgement?

_items.text: Judge each task on its own: use AI where it helps, keep it out where the struggle is the learning, and protect your privacy and integrity throughout.
_items.feedback: Yes. That runs the whole judgement, task by task, across the term.

_items.text: Use AI for every task in {{context}}, since it saves the most time.
_items.feedback: Some tasks are meant to build your own skill; the first move is to judge fit.

_items.text: Avoid AI entirely in {{context}}, whatever the task.
_items.feedback: A blanket ban is as unthinking as blanket use.

_items.text: Use AI freely in {{context}}, as long as you never tell anyone.
_items.feedback: Use that has to be hidden is a sign it is not honest.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Responsible judgement weighs each task on its own and protects learning, privacy and integrity.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Blanket use, a blanket ban and secrecy all replace judgement with an unthinking rule.
_incorrect.final: You judge each task on its own, using AI where it helps and keeping it out where the struggle is the learning, while protecting privacy and integrity. Blanket rules and secrecy are not responsible use.

displayTitle: Why is responsible AI use best seen as one judgement rather than a single rule such as 'always declare it'?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Why is responsible use best seen as one judgement rather than a single rule?

_items.text: Because a use can be declared yet still harm your learning, privacy or the environment, so several things are weighed together.
_items.feedback: Yes. One rule cannot protect everything at once.

_items.text: Because declaring use is never needed once you use AI responsibly.
_items.feedback: Declaring use is often part of responsible use.

_items.text: Because one judgement means you can skip checking the output.
_items.feedback: Checking the output stays part of the judgement.

_items.text: Because weighing things up takes less care than a rule.
_items.feedback: It takes more care, not less.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Responsible use weighs learning, integrity, privacy and impact together.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about everything responsible use has to protect at once.

displayTitle: A student needs deep, uninterrupted thinking for a reflective task and does not fully understand a tool's output on it. What does responsible judgement suggest?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What does responsible judgement suggest for a reflective task the student does not understand the output on?

_items.text: Keep AI out of this task: the struggle is the learning, and not understanding the output is a reason to stop.
_items.feedback: Yes. This is a task to do without AI.

_items.text: Use the tool anyway, since it saves time.
_items.feedback: Saving time is not the test; the struggle here is the learning.

_items.text: Use the output without understanding it, as long as it is reworded.
_items.feedback: Not understanding the output is a reason to stop, not to reword.

_items.text: Use AI because every task is improved by it.
_items.feedback: Not every task is; some are meant to build your own thinking.

_feedback.correct: That's right. When the struggle is the learning and the output is not understood, keep AI out.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about when responsible use means not using AI at all.

title: Use AI as a partner
displayTitle: Use AI as a partner
body: The difference between learning and offloading is in how you use the tool.

_items.title: Do
_items.text: Ask AI to explain, quiz you, or critique your draft, then do the thinking yourself.

_items.title: Do not
_items.text: Paste its answer in as your own, or treat it as a final authority.

_items.title: Tip
_items.text: Ask for the method, not the answer, so you learn how to get there.

title: Order the steps of checking an AI claim
displayTitle: Order the steps of checking an AI claim
body: When an AI states something as fact, you check it. Put the steps in order.
instruction: Drag the steps into the right order, then select Submit.

_items.text: Identify the exact claim the AI has made.
Check whether it gives a source you can follow.
Find an independent, trusted source on the same point.
Compare the two and note where they differ.
Decide whether to use, verify further, or reject the claim.

_feedback.title: Checking a claim
_feedback.correct: That is the order. Name the claim, look for its source, find an independent one, compare, then decide.

_incorrect.final: Not quite. Start by naming the claim, then look for sources before you compare and decide.
_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what you need before you can compare anything, and try again.

title: Spot the failure
displayTitle: Spot the failure
body: AI answers can look complete and still be wrong. Work through the situation.
instruction: Choose a response to see what happens, then follow where it leads. Each choice has consequences.

n1.body: You ask AI for three studies on your topic. It returns three, each with an author, a journal and a year, all sounding plausible. What do you do?

_choices.text: Cite all three straight away, since they look complete.
_choices.consequence: They look complete, but AI invents references that read perfectly. You have not checked whether any of them exist.

_choices.text: Search for each one in the library before using it.
_choices.consequence: You find that one is invented and drop it. The other two are real journal articles.

n2.body: The two remaining papers are real. The AI also summarised what each one argues, and you want to use those points. What do you do?

_choices.text: Read the two papers yourself to confirm they say what the AI claimed.
_choices.consequence: Right. A real source can still be misrepresented by an AI summary; now you know the points hold up.

_choices.text: Use the AI's summaries, since the papers are definitely real.
_choices.consequence: The sources are real, but a summary you have not checked can still distort what a paper actually says.

nRecover.body: You have cited all three. A coursemate mentions that AI often invents references. You still have time before the deadline. What do you do?

_choices.text: Leave it, because the references looked fine to you.
_choices.consequence: You keep references you never verified.

_choices.text: Check each one in the library before you submit.
_choices.consequence: You catch the invented reference and remove it, then turn to the two that are real.

nGood.body: You confirmed that each source is real and that it says what you thought. That habit protects your work from AI's two most common failures: invented sources and misread ones.

nNeutral.body: The sources are real, which matters. But an AI summary you have not checked can still misrepresent a paper. Read the source before you rely on its argument.

nPoor.body: Fabricated references are a known failure mode, and two of these do not exist. They are now in your work. Always confirm a source is real before you rely on it.

title: Before you rely on an AI answer
displayTitle: Checklist: Before you rely on an AI answer
body: Run these checks before you treat an AI answer as something you can use.
instruction: Tick each item once you have done it.

_items.text: Have I checked the claim against a trusted source?
Have I confirmed any reference actually exists?
Have I asked whether the answer could be out of date?
Have I watched for a confident tone hiding a weak answer?
Can I explain the answer in my own words?
